title: Customer Service Excellence and Customer Acquisition

questions.stem: The 'ultimate moment of truth' in a life insurance customer's experience is generally considered to be:

opts.x: The moment the policyholder receives their first annual benefit statement.
The first premium collection by direct debit.
The claim payment, which tests whether the insurer's promise was genuine.
The product presentation by the insurance agent.

questions.answer: (C) The claim payment, which tests whether the insurer's promise was genuine.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

The 'moment of truth' concept in service management identifies the interactions that most powerfully define a customer's perception of a service provider. In life insurance, the claim payment is the definitive test: the policyholder (or their beneficiary) has paid premiums for years in exchange for a promise. The claim is the moment when that promise is either honoured or broken. Every other interaction (policy issuance, annual statements, premium receipts) is subordinate — it is the claim that determines whether the customer (or their family) was wise to trust the insurer.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The annual benefit statement confirms the policy is in force and reports accumulated values — an important servicing interaction but not the definitive trust test.
(B) The first premium collection confirms the payment mechanism is working — an administrative milestone, not a trust-testing moment.
(D) The product presentation is the acquisition moment — trust has not yet been established. It is the beginning of the relationship, not its defining test.

questions.stem: The Net Promoter Score (NPS) is calculated by:

opts.x: Subtracting the percentage of dissatisfied claimants from the percentage of satisfied claimants.
Subtracting the percentage of Detractors (scoring 0–6) from the percentage of Promoters (scoring 9–10).
Averaging all customer satisfaction scores collected in the relevant period.
Dividing the number of referred new customers by the total number of existing policyholders.

questions.answer: (B) Subtracting the percentage of Detractors (those scoring 0–6 on the recommendation question) from the percentage of Promoters (those scoring 9–10).

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

NPS is calculated from a single question: 'How likely are you to recommend [Insurer Name] to a friend or family member?' scored 0–10. Respondents are classified:
• Promoters: scored 9–10 (loyal enthusiasts who actively recommend)
• Passives: scored 7–8 (satisfied but not enthusiastic — excluded from the NPS calculation)
• Detractors: scored 0–6 (unhappy customers who may actively warn others against the insurer)

NPS = % Promoters − % Detractors. A score of +30 indicates significantly more Promoters than Detractors. Nigerian life insurers typically have negative NPS scores — more people warn others against them than recommend them.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The satisfaction vs dissatisfaction ratio is a different measurement framework — simpler but less predictive of loyalty and referral behaviour than NPS.
(C) Averaging all scores (the mean approach) does not distinguish between the very satisfied (Promoters) and the very dissatisfied (Detractors) — both groups have disproportionate behavioural impact on word-of-mouth.
(D) Dividing referrals by policyholders is a referral rate metric — related to NPS outcomes but not the NPS calculation itself.

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025's three-tier complaints redress mechanism, if a policyholder is dissatisfied with the insurer's internal resolution, the next step is:

opts.x: To file a claim in the Federal High Court.
To refer the complaint to NAICOM's Consumer Protection Department.
To contact the insurer's Board of Directors directly.
To notify the Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA) of the dispute.

questions.answer: (B) To refer the complaint to NAICOM's Consumer Protection Department.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 establishes a three-tier complaints resolution framework:
Tier 1: Internal resolution — the insurer's own complaints team attempts to resolve within a defined period (typically 15 working days).
Tier 2: NAICOM Consumer Protection Department — if the insurer's resolution is unsatisfactory, the policyholder escalates to NAICOM. NAICOM investigates and issues a finding. This is the regulatory escalation stage.
Tier 3: The courts — if NAICOM's finding is not accepted or does not resolve the matter, litigation in the courts is available as the final recourse.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Going directly to the Federal High Court bypasses both internal resolution and the NAICOM escalation stage — it is premature, expensive, and not the intended first step.
(C) Contacting the Board of Directors directly is not a formal complaints escalation step in NIIRA 2025's mechanism — though a policyholder may write to the Chairman as a matter of corporate governance, this is not the regulatory escalation pathway.
(D) The NIA is the insurers' trade association — it has no formal role in individual policyholder complaints resolution.

questions.stem: A policyholder calls to update their beneficiary. The agent cannot resolve it immediately and promises to call back within 24 hours. When the agent does not call back and the policyholder calls again the following day, this represents a failure of:

opts.x: The insurer's reinsurance management obligations.
The First Contact Resolution principle and the Service Level Agreement for callback commitments.
The insurer's NIIRA 2025 mandatory policy filing requirement.
The policyholder's duty of disclosure under the policy contract.

questions.answer: (B) The First Contact Resolution principle and the Service Level Agreement for callback commitments.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

First Contact Resolution (FCR) is the principle that customer queries are resolved at the first point of contact wherever possible, without requiring the customer to call back or follow up. In this case, FCR was not achieved — the beneficiary update required a callback promise. The agent's failure to call back within 24 hours is a Service Level Agreement (SLA) breach: the insurer's contact centre SLA defines the maximum response time for different interaction types and callback commitments are binding service obligations. The policyholder's need to call back represents both a customer experience failure and an SLA failure.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Reinsurance management obligations relate to the insurer's cession of risk to reinsurers — entirely unrelated to a contact centre callback failure.
(C) Policy filing requirements relate to NAICOM product approval — also unrelated.
(D) The duty of disclosure is the insured's pre-contract obligation — not relevant to a post-issuance beneficiary update interaction.

questions.stem: In insurance customer retention, a 'conservation programme' is best described as:

opts.x: An environmental sustainability programme.
A structured set of interventions designed to retain policyholders who have indicated they wish to surrender or cancel their policy.
A programme for conserving the insurer's capital reserves in periods of adverse mortality experience.
An annual review of all in-force policies to ensure coverage levels remain adequate.

questions.answer: (B) A structured set of interventions designed to retain policyholders who have indicated they wish to surrender or cancel their policy.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

A conservation programme in insurance specifically refers to the set of actions taken to prevent a policyholder from surrendering or lapsing their policy. When a policyholder contacts the insurer to request a surrender or when their premium payment indicates they are about to lapse, a conservation specialist intervenes with a structured conversation covering: understanding the reason for the proposed surrender; exploring alternatives (premium holiday; paid-up conversion; loan against policy; sum assured reduction); and attempting to resolve the underlying issue (financial pressure, service dissatisfaction, product misunderstanding) that is driving the surrender decision.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Environmental sustainability has no connection to insurance conservation programmes.
(C) Capital reserve management is a financial function — not the definition of a customer conservation programme.
(D) Annual coverage reviews are a customer servicing activity — proactive and positive, not triggered by a surrender risk signal.

questions.stem:
A life insurer has the following monthly CX performance data: NPS = +8; CSAT (post-claims) = 3.2/5; FCR rate = 58%; claims settlement time (average) = 22 days; lapse rate (month-13 persistency) = 62%; complaint volume: 180 complaints received, 145 resolved within SLA.
(a) Assess each metric against the targets discussed in this chapter and identify the two most critical performance gaps.
(b) For each of the two critical gaps, describe the root cause investigation process the CX director should initiate.
(c) Describe three specific process or technology interventions that could improve the CSAT (post-claims) score to 4.0/5 or above within six months.
(d) Explain how the lapse rate performance is connected to the NPS score and describe the causal mechanism.

model.h: Part (a) — Performance Assessment and Critical Gaps

rows: BELOW TARGET (best practice target: +20). Positive but low — more Promoters than Detractors, but the margin is narrow. Indicates the majority of customers are Passives — not actively recommending or condemning the insurer.

CRITICAL GAP #1. Target: 4.0/5 or above. At 3.2, a significant proportion of claimants are dissatisfied with the claims experience — the most important customer experience moment in life insurance. This is the primary trust-building failure point.
BELOW TARGET (target: 70%+). 42% of customer queries require multiple contacts. This is operationally inefficient and frustrating for customers — but secondary to the claims and persistency gaps.
WITHIN NIIRA 2025 mandate (60 days) but 22 days is suboptimal — target best practice is 10–14 days. Below the 30-day legal maximum.
CRITICAL GAP #2. Target: 70%+. 38% of policyholders from 13 months ago have lapsed — a level that is eroding the renewal book at a rate that likely exceeds new business generation.
Below best practice (95%+ target). 19.4% of complainants are not receiving timely resolution — each represents a potential NAICOM escalation and a Detractor NPS score.

model.h: Part (b) — Root Cause Investigation for Each Critical Gap

Critical Gap 1 — CSAT post-claims 3.2/5:
Root cause investigation process:
1. Claims experience survey deep-dive: Segment the CSAT data by claim type (death claim; critical illness; survival benefit), claim outcome (paid; declined; reduced), and claim processing time (under 10 days; 10–22 days; over 22 days). Identify which segments are driving the low score — is it declined claims, slow processing, or communication quality?
2. Claims staff competency review: Mystery customer calls to the claims team assessing: empathy and communication quality; accuracy of information provided; proactivity in explaining next steps.
3. Documentation request analysis: Are claimants submitting correct documents first time, or are multiple document requests (each adding delay and frustration) contributing to dissatisfaction?

Critical Gap 2 — Month-13 persistency 62%:
Root cause investigation process:
1. Lapse cohort analysis: What is the profile of lapsed policies? Agent of sale; product type; customer income segment; channel (bancassurance vs agency vs digital)? Identifying the highest-lapse cohort focuses the intervention.
2. Agent-level persistency breakdown: Pull the 13-month persistency by individual agent. A small number of agents may be generating the majority of lapses — indicating mis-selling by specific agents rather than a systemic problem.
3. Exit call analysis for surrendered policies: Review recordings of calls where customers requested surrender. What was the most frequently stated reason?
Part (c) — Three Interventions to Improve Post-Claims CSAT to 4.0/5

1. Proactive claims status communication: Implement an automated claims update system (WhatsApp/SMS) that provides the claimant with a progress update every 5 business days during the claims process — 'Your claim reference [X] is being assessed. Our target is to complete by [date].' Research consistently shows that proactive communication improves customer satisfaction even when the resolution time is unchanged — customers feel less anxious when they know the process is progressing.

2. Empathy-focused claims communication training: Conduct a 2-day structured training programme for all claims staff on communicating with bereaved families and critically ill claimants. Train on: active listening; avoiding policy jargon in verbal communication; the specific language that conveys empathy vs bureaucratic detachment ('I understand this is a very difficult time' vs 'Your claim is being processed according to company procedures'). Target: 0.4 CSAT improvement from communication quality alone.

3. Decline decision communication redesign: When claims are declined, redesign the communication to: explain the specific policy clause that applies; provide the insurer's rationale in plain language; explicitly state the right of appeal and the NAICOM escalation pathway. A declined claim communicated with clarity and empathy generates less dissatisfaction than a declined claim communicated in legalistic, jargon-heavy language.
Part (d) — Connection Between Lapse Rate and NPS

The connection between month-13 persistency (62%) and NPS (+8) is direct and bidirectional:

Lapse → NPS (negative impact pathway): A policyholder who lapses in year 1 — especially one who received a low surrender value after paying premiums for 13 months — has a high probability of becoming a Detractor (NPS 0–6). Their experience confirms the trust deficit narrative: 'I paid, nothing happened, I got very little back.' These Detractors actively warn family and community members against the insurer — generating the negative word-of-mouth that suppresses new business conversion.

NPS → Lapse (feedback pathway): A policyholder with a poor CX experience (NPS Detractor score) is more likely to lapse their policy as a signal of disengagement — 'I have no confidence in this insurer; I may as well stop paying.' The relationship between NPS and lapse intent is well-documented in insurance retention research.

Causal mechanism: Both lapse and NPS are consequences of the same underlying failure — the gap between the experience the customer was sold (during the product presentation) and the experience they actually received (in policy servicing, claims communication, and contact centre interactions). Closing this gap improves both persistency and NPS simultaneously.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer has 85,000 active individual life policyholders. In the past 12 months, 9,350 policies have lapsed. The average first-year premium on a new policy is ₦240,000, and the average CAC per new policy acquired through the retail agency channel is ₦65,000.
(a) Calculate the annualised premium income lost from the 9,350 lapses.
(b) Calculate the acquisition cost to replace the lapsed policies with equivalent new policies.
(c) Explain why the cost of preventing lapses is typically lower than the cost of replacing them with new policies, and describe the financial case for investing in a proactive lapse management programme.
(d) Design the key components of a lapse management programme for this insurer, specifying the triggers, the interventions, and the performance metrics.

model.h: Part (a) — Annual Premium Income Lost from 9,350 Lapses

Assuming the lapsed policies' average renewal premium is equivalent to the average first-year premium:
Annual premium lost = 9,350 lapsed policies × ₦240,000 average annual premium
Annual premium lost = ₦2,244,000,000 (₦2.244 billion)

Note: In practice, renewal premiums may differ from FYP — if the lapsed portfolio includes older policies whose premiums have escalated, the actual premium loss would be higher.
Part (b) — Acquisition Cost to Replace Lapsed Policies

To replace 9,350 lapsed policies with equivalent new policies via the retail agency channel:
Acquisition cost = 9,350 new policies × ₦65,000 CAC per policy
Acquisition cost = ₦607,750,000 (₦607.75 million)

This is the additional cost the insurer must incur simply to return to its prior portfolio size — before any growth.
Part (c) — Why Prevention Costs Less Than Replacement

The financial case for lapse prevention:

1. Acquisition cost avoidance: The insurer spends ₦65,000 to acquire each new customer. A conservation specialist can typically prevent a lapse for ₦5,000–₦15,000 (the cost of the conservation call, the conservation specialist's time, and any retention incentive offered). Preventing one lapse saves ₦50,000–₦60,000 in avoided acquisition cost.

2. Renewal premium recovery: A prevented lapse retains the annual renewal premium (₦240,000). Replacing the lapsed policy generates a new first-year premium (₦240,000) but at ₦65,000 acquisition cost — a net cost of ₦65,000 vs a net gain from retention.

3. Lifetime value: A retained policyholder who is in their 5th year of a 20-year policy has 15 more years of premium and relationship potential. A new replacement policyholder resets the relationship to year 1 — including the high-lapse-risk early years.

Financial case: If the insurer invests ₦100m in a proactive lapse management programme that reduces lapses from 9,350 to 7,500 (a reduction of 1,850 lapses), the savings are:
• Avoided acquisition cost: 1,850 × ₦65,000 = ₦120.25m
• Retained premium income: 1,850 × ₦240,000 = ₦444m additional annual premium retention
• Net financial return on ₦100m investment: ₦120.25m acquisition cost saving alone exceeds the investment in year 1.
Part (d) — Key Components of a Lapse Management Programme

rows: Digital: No mobile app login for 60 days; missed premium payment SMS acknowledgement; surrender enquiry received. Call centre: inbound call expressing dissatisfaction with product or service. Agent-reported: agent flags a customer they believe is considering lapsing.

High-value policies (above ₦500,000 annual premium): immediate personal call from a senior conservation specialist. Mid-value (₦100k–₦500k): outreach within 3 business days. Lower-value (below ₦100k): automated SMS/WhatsApp conservation campaign with human escalation if not resolved within 7 days.

Premium holiday: offer a 2-month premium suspension for customers citing temporary financial difficulty. Paid-up conversion: for customers who genuinely cannot sustain premiums — retain the policy at a reduced sum assured rather than losing it entirely. Loan against policy: for whole life and endowment policies with accumulated cash value. Service recovery: where the lapse trigger is a poor service experience — immediate escalation to a senior service officer with authority to offer remediation.

Conservation rate: % of at-risk policies successfully retained. Revenue saved: additional premium income from conserved policies (gross). Cost per prevented lapse: total programme cost ÷ number of lapses prevented. 13-month persistency rate improvement: measured quarterly against a baseline.

questions.stem:
A 78-year-old retired teacher contacts the insurer’s contact centre to enquire about surrendering her whole life policy. She has held the policy for 23 years and paid premiums totalling ₦8.4 million. Her current surrender value is ₦16,500,000. She says she needs money urgently because her son is asking her to contribute to a business venture.
(a) Identify all the vulnerability indicators present in this customer interaction.
(b) Describe the adapted service protocol the contact centre agent should follow.
(c) What alternatives to immediate surrender should the agent present to this customer, and how should each be explained?
(d) What does the insurer’s duty of care under NIIRA 2025 require in this situation?

model.h: Part (a) — Vulnerability Indicators

Multiple vulnerability indicators are present simultaneously in this interaction:

1. Age: 78 years old — she is in the category of older customers who may experience reduced cognitive capacity, greater susceptibility to influence, and reduced ability to evaluate complex financial transactions under pressure.

2. Third-party pressure: The son is 'asking her to contribute to a business venture' — this is a classic financial elder abuse indicator. The customer did not originate the desire to surrender; a third party is prompting the financial decision for their own benefit.

3. Urgency framing: 'She needs money urgently' — urgency is a manipulation technique that overrides careful deliberation. A genuinely sound financial decision does not require eliminating the customer's time to think.

4. Long-term policy surrender: She has held this policy for 23 years — surrendering it destroys a long-term financial asset that she cannot rebuild at age 78. The irreversibility of the decision is a vulnerability amplifier.

5. Potential misunderstanding of alternatives: She may not be aware of alternatives (policy loan, partial withdrawal) that could provide the needed funds without surrendering the policy entirely.
Part (b) — Adapted Service Protocol

The contact centre agent should follow a vulnerable customer protocol:

Step 1 — Flag the interaction: Immediately flag this call for supervisor awareness and do not process the surrender request on the initial call.

Step 2 — Empathetic exploration: 'I'd like to help you with this. Before we talk about the surrender, can I ask — has there been anything specific that's come up financially that's making you need the money urgently? I want to make sure we find the best solution for you.'

Step 3 — Explore the nature of the need: Is the son present? (If so, the agent should ask to speak with the customer privately.) What is the specific amount needed? (It may be less than ₦16.5m.) Is there a deadline?

Step 4 — Present alternatives without immediately processing: 'Before we complete the surrender, I'd like to share a few options with you that might give you access to the money you need while protecting your policy. Would that be okay?'

Step 5 — Cooling-off recommendation: 'Given the long-term nature of this policy, our protocol for longstanding policyholders is to give a 5-day reflection period before processing a surrender. I'll send you the surrender value confirmation in writing, along with the alternatives, so you can review everything carefully. Can I call you back in 5 days?'

Step 6 — Document: Record all details of the interaction, flag the vulnerability indicators, and escalate to the conservation team.
Part (c) — Alternatives to Immediate Surrender

1. Policy loan: A whole life policy with a surrender value of ₦16.5m almost certainly has a substantial accumulated cash value against which a policy loan can be arranged. The customer borrows against the policy (typically up to 80–90% of surrender value) — in this case, potentially ₦13–15m. The policy remains in force; the loan is repaid (with interest) or deducted from the death benefit. If the purpose of the funds is a one-time business contribution, a policy loan is far superior to surrender because the life cover remains intact and the loan can be repaid if the business generates returns.

2. Partial surrender/partial withdrawal: Rather than surrendering the entire ₦16.5m value, the customer withdraws only the amount actually needed for the son's business — preserving the balance of the policy's value and the life cover.

3. Reduced paid-up conversion: If premium payment is the issue (which it does not appear to be in this case), converting to paid-up status would maintain a reduced death benefit without further premiums. This is less relevant here but should be noted for completeness.
Part (d) — NIIRA 2025 Duty of Care

NIIRA 2025's consumer protection framework and the TCF principle impose a specific duty of care for vulnerable customers:

1. Vulnerability identification: NIIRA 2025 requires insurers to have documented policies for identifying and serving vulnerable customers. The contact centre agent must be trained to recognise the vulnerability indicators present in this interaction and follow the prescribed protocol.

2. Non-pressured decision-making: The insurer must ensure that the customer's decision is her own — not coerced by a third party. Where third-party pressure is suspected, the insurer has a duty to provide the customer with information and time to make an independent, informed decision.

3. Proportionate advice: NIIRA 2025's TCF principle requires that the customer is advised of all options relevant to her situation — not just the one she is requesting. Failing to present the policy loan option to a customer who then surrenders a 23-year policy unnecessarily would be a TCF failure.

4. Safeguarding referral: If the agent has reasonable grounds to believe the customer is being financially abused by the son, NIIRA 2025's consumer protection obligations — combined with NAICOM's Vulnerable Customer Guidelines — require the insurer to consider referring the matter to an appropriate authority, and at minimum to delay processing until the customer has had the opportunity to seek independent advice.

questions.stem: NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection framework represents the most comprehensive statutory codification of policyholder rights in Nigerian insurance history. Critically evaluate whether the framework is sufficient to address the customer experience failures that have characterised the Nigerian life insurance market, and whether it will be effectively enforced. In your answer, discuss: the gap between the framework’s written requirements and the operational capability of the average Nigerian life insurer to comply with them; the enforcement tools available to NAICOM and the conditions under which they are likely to be deployed; the role of the insurer’s own CX investment and cultural commitment in delivering outcomes that go beyond minimum regulatory compliance; and the metrics by which the market’s CX improvement over the next five years should be measured.

model.h: Thesis

NIIRA 2025's consumer protection framework is a significant legislative achievement. It creates the legal architecture for treating Nigerian insurance customers fairly. But legislation creates obligations — it does not create capabilities, incentives, or culture. The gap between the framework's requirements and the operational reality of many Nigerian life insurers is large, and the enforcement infrastructure to bridge this gap is still being built.
Gap Between Framework Requirements and Operational Capability

NIIRA 2025's requirements include: mandatory 60-day claims settlement; benefit illustration delivery before sale; cooling-off rights; mandatory service level standards; accessible complaints resolution; and TCF as a statutory principle.

Compliance capability gap for the average Nigerian life insurer:
1. Technology deficit: Many Nigerian life insurers operate on legacy policy administration systems that cannot generate automated claims status updates, trigger proactive communication workflows, or produce digitally delivered benefit illustrations on demand. The 60-day claims mandate requires workflow management systems that a significant proportion of the industry has not yet built.

2. Human capital deficit: The TCF principle requires insurance sales and service staff who can assess suitability, recognise vulnerability, explain benefits accurately, and handle complaints empathetically. Many Nigerian insurers have not invested in the training and competency development that this standard requires.

3. Data infrastructure deficit: Effective consumer protection compliance requires data — knowing which claims are approaching the 60-day deadline; which customers have not received their policy documents; which complaints are approaching their SLA deadline. Insurers without real-time operational dashboards will breach these requirements without knowing it until after the fact.
NAICOM's Enforcement Tools and Likely Deployment

NAICOM's enforcement toolkit under NIIRA 2025 includes: financial consequences (compound interest and administrative sanctions for claims delays; fixed amounts for other breaches); naming of non-compliant insurers publicly; licence suspension for persistent violators; criminal liability for directors.

Likely deployment pattern: NAICOM's enforcement will be prioritised toward the most visible and measurable breaches — particularly the 60-day claims mandate (which is easy to monitor through quarterly claims data returns) and advertising standard violations (which are publicly visible). Less visible breaches (suitability assessment failures; inadequate benefit illustration delivery) are harder to detect through supervisory reporting and require field inspection to identify.

Enforcement constraints: NAICOM's market conduct inspection team is small relative to 50+ licensed life insurers. Comprehensive on-site inspection of each insurer's CX practices is not achievable on an annual basis. Mandatory customer-outcome reporting (all insurers submit quarterly claims, complaint, and persistency data to NAICOM) would enable NAICOM to deploy its inspection resources more efficiently — focusing on outliers.
Role of Insurer CX Investment

Regulatory compliance alone will not deliver the CX improvement the Nigerian market needs. The insurers that will define the market's next decade are those that invest in CX as a commercial strategy — not because NAICOM requires it, but because they have understood that customer retention, net promoter scores, and referral business are the most cost-efficient growth strategies available.

The CX investments that generate the highest returns:
1. Claims process excellence: A claims team that consistently settles within 14 days (vs the NIIRA 2025 60-day mandate) generates NPS improvement, referrals, and renewal premium retention that more than pays for the investment.
2. Proactive digital communication: WhatsApp-based policy anniversary messages, premium receipt confirmations, and claims status updates cost very little but significantly improve customer satisfaction and reduce inbound contact centre load.
3. Conservation programme: A well-designed lapse management programme generates a financial return that exceeds its investment in year 1 — the financial case is overwhelming for any insurer that has quantified the cost of lapsed policies.
Metrics for Measuring CX Improvement Over Five Years

Industry-level metrics NAICOM should track and publish annually:
1. Industry average 13-month persistency rate: Target trajectory from current ~62% to 72% by 2030.
2. Claims settlement within 60 days: % of all life insurance claims settled within the statutory mandate. Target: 95%+ by 2027.
3. Complaint volume per 10,000 policies: A declining ratio indicates improving customer experience at scale.
4. NPS by product class: An annual industry NPS survey (conducted by an independent research house) comparing individual life, group life, and annuity NPS scores across licensed insurers. Public results create competitive pressure for CX improvement.
5. Unclaimed funds registry growth rate: If the Unclaimed Funds Registry continues to grow, it indicates that beneficiaries are not being found and contacted proactively. A declining growth rate would indicate improving claims outreach.

Insurer-level metrics that Boards should receive quarterly: CSAT post-claims; FCR rate; complaints resolved within SLA; NPS movement; lapse rate trend.

questions.stem: ‘Customer retention is the most undervalued and underinvested function in Nigerian life insurance. The commercial logic for retention investment is overwhelming — yet most Nigerian life insurers continue to invest ten times more in acquisition than in retention, producing a leaky bucket in which new premium income pours in at the top while lapse losses drain from the bottom at a rate that negates much of the acquisition effort.’ Critically evaluate this proposition. In your answer, examine the evidence on the relative financial value of retention versus acquisition in life insurance; analyse the structural and cultural reasons why Nigerian life insurance companies systematically under-invest in retention relative to the financial return; describe the components of a best-practice retention programme and the investment required; and identify the metrics, governance structures, and incentive realignments that would shift management attention toward retention as a strategic priority equivalent to new business growth.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition is correct and the financial evidence is compelling. The systematic under-investment in retention relative to acquisition in Nigerian life insurance reflects a combination of structural incentive misalignment, measurement failure, and cultural overvaluation of new business that is common in growth-stage insurance markets globally but is particularly acute in Nigeria given the market's persistency crisis.
Financial Evidence on Retention vs Acquisition Value

Life insurance economics make the financial case for retention starkly:

1. Customer lifetime value (CLTV): A policyholder who maintains a ₦240,000 annual premium for 10 years generates ₦2.4m in total premium. A policyholder who lapses at month 13 generates ₦240,000. The 10-year policyholder generates 10× the revenue — but acquisition cost is identical (₦65,000 each).

2. Marginal cost of retention vs acquisition: Preventing a lapse through proactive conservation costs ₦5,000–₦15,000 per policy saved. Acquiring a replacement policyholder costs ₦65,000. The retention ROI is 4–13× superior to the acquisition ROI.

3. In-force book value: The insurer's most important balance sheet asset is its in-force premium book. A book of ₦50bn AFYP with 62% persistency generates ₦31bn in renewal premium. The same book with 75% persistency generates ₦37.5bn — a ₦6.5bn improvement in annual renewal income from a 13-point persistency improvement.

4. The leaky bucket analogy: If the insurer writes ₦120bn in new business annually but loses ₦80bn in lapsed renewal premium, the net growth is only ₦40bn. The ₦80bn acquisition cost generates a much smaller net revenue increase than it appears — because lapses are draining the in-force book at nearly the same rate as new business fills it.
Structural and Cultural Reasons for Under-Investment in Retention

1. Incentive misalignment at every level: CEO compensation is linked to new business targets, not persistency targets. Branch managers are measured on AFYP, not renewals. Agents earn the majority of their income in year 1 — not years 2–10. Every level of the distribution and management hierarchy is financially incentivised for acquisition, not retention.

2. Measurement failure: Many Nigerian life insurers do not calculate their true lapse cost — they track lapse rates as a percentage but not the naira value of premium income lost from lapses. If the leaky bucket cost is not quantified and placed beside the acquisition spend, the financial case for retention investment is invisible to decision-makers.

3. Cultural overvaluation of new business: 'New business' has cultural cachet in insurance organisations — it is celebrated, recognised, and rewarded. 'Retention' is viewed as a defensive, administrative function. This cultural hierarchy shapes budget allocation decisions even when the financial data would support the opposite allocation.

4. Short-term financial reporting: Insurance company financial reporting (both internal management accounts and NAICOM regulatory returns) emphasises premium income growth — which is heavily influenced by new business. Renewal income, lapse ratios, and retention programme ROI are not prominent metrics in most Nigerian life insurer management reporting.
Components of a Best-Practice Retention Programme

1. Early warning system: A predictive lapse propensity model that uses policy data (days since last engagement, payment method, agent tenure, product type, customer income segment) to generate a weekly 'at-risk' policy list for proactive conservation outreach.

2. Segmented conservation team: A dedicated team of conservation specialists (separate from the contact centre queue) who are specifically trained and resourced for retention conversations — not generic customer service interactions.

3. Graduated intervention protocol: Light touch (automated WhatsApp/SMS) for low-risk policies approaching premium due dates; personal call for policies showing first missed premium signs; senior conservation specialist for high-value or long-tenure policies at risk.

4. Retention incentive toolkit: Premium holiday (2–3 months without lapse); loan against policy; sum assured reduction; paid-up conversion with loyalty recognition. The conservation specialist must have clear authority to offer these without requiring management approval on each case — approval delays lose the conservation opportunity.

5. Post-conservation follow-up: A conserved policyholder who experienced financial difficulty should receive a follow-up contact 6 months later — both to confirm the policy is still in force and to offer additional support if needed.
Metrics, Governance, and Incentive Realignment

Metrics the Board should receive monthly:
1. 13-month persistency rate (overall and by channel, product, and agent tier)
2. Value of lapsed premium (₦m per month) and trend
3. Conservation programme success rate (% of at-risk policies retained)
4. Net policyholder count movement (new policies issued minus lapses)

Governance restructuring:
1. Appoint a Chief Retention Officer (or designate retention as a formal responsibility of the CMO/COO) with a defined retention budget and retention targets.
2. Include persistency KPIs in the Board's balanced scorecard alongside new business targets.
3. Require the CEO's annual performance review to include a persistency target alongside new business and profitability targets.

Incentive realignment:
1. Introduce renewal commission that grows with policy tenure — an agent whose policyholder is still active at year 5 earns a higher renewal commission rate than for a year-2 policyholder. This creates a multi-year financial interest in retention for the agent.
2. Branch manager bonus: 40% weighted to new business AFYP; 40% weighted to 13-month persistency rate of new business written; 20% weighted to in-force book renewal income. This replaces the AFYP-only bonus structure.
3. CEO long-term incentive plan (LTIP): Include a 3-year persistency improvement target as a vesting condition alongside revenue and profitability targets.
